Hail, Wind and Your Solar Panels: How They're Tested and What to Look For

Ice balls at 51 mph, load ratings in pascals, and why tilt matters. A plain guide to storm-ready solar.

Amp Voltsworth

Anybody who's lived through a few summers in the Wabash Valley has heard hail on the roof. So it's a fair question when you're thinking about solar: what happens to the panels when a storm rolls through?

Short answer: certified panels are tested for it. Here's what those tests are, what the ratings on a spec sheet mean, and how a good install adds margin.

The Track Record

The U.S. Department of Energy's Federal Energy Management Program puts it plainly: historically, solar modules have survived the majority of hail events they've experienced. DOE says the real trouble has come in areas that have seen very large hail, bigger than 1¾ inches (44 mm) across. That's why the testing and the design choices below matter.

How Panels Are Hail-Tested

The baseline is the hail test in IEC 61215, the international design-qualification standard for solar modules. According to DOE, to be "hail certified" a module has to come through 11 strikes from 25 mm (1-inch) ice balls fired at 23 meters per second, about 51 mph, with no visible damage and less than 5% loss of power.

That's the minimum. IEC also lists optional, tougher tests with bigger ice balls at higher speeds:

  • 35 mm at 27.2 m/s
  • 45 mm at 30.7 m/s
  • 55 mm at 33.9 m/s
  • 65 mm at 36.7 m/s
  • 76 mm at 39.5 m/s

DOE notes that manufacturers rarely publish those higher results, so you may have to ask. It also points to advanced programs such as RETC's Hail Durability Test, PVEL's Hail Stress Sequence and FM Global Standard 4478, plus ASTM E1038 testing for hail from 25 to 85 mm.

Reading the Strength Ratings on a Spec Sheet

Hail isn't the only load a panel has to carry. Snow pushes down. Wind pushes and pulls. Spec sheets list those as mechanical loads in pascals (Pa) or pounds per square foot. As an example only, not a recommendation, here's what the Qcells Q.TRON BLK M-G2+ datasheet (April 2026) lists:

  • Front glass: 3.2 mm thermally pre-stressed glass.
  • Max. design load: 5,400 Pa push (113 lb/ft²) and 2,400 Pa pull (50 lb/ft²).
  • Max. test load: 8,100 Pa push (169 lb/ft²) and 3,600 Pa pull (75 lb/ft²).
  • Certifications: UL 61730, IEC 61215:2021 and IEC 61730:2023.

That 3.2 mm glass number is worth checking on any panel. DOE recommends modules with at least 3.2 mm front glass for hail resilience, and says glass thinner than that is typically heat-treated rather than tempered, which isn't as strong. DOE also suggests choosing framed modules with a stronger frame, and notes that smaller-format modules may be at lower risk than large-format ones.

Where the Install Makes a Difference

Here's a detail most folks never hear. DOE says the most damaging hail falls closer to straight down, so steeper tilt angles reduce the chance of a direct, perpendicular hit. The trade-off, DOE adds, is that a steeper tilt sees higher wind loads, so the racking has to be built for it.

That's one more reason we like ground mounts on rural properties. On a ground mount, the tilt is a design choice instead of whatever pitch your roof happens to be. The structure underneath matters just as much. Racking makers publish their own guidance. IronRidge, named here as an example only, not a recommendation, publishes foundation guidance that depends on soil class, and says to consult an engineer for anything outside their certification letters. Matching the footings to your soil is part of doing the job right.

DOE also suggests looking up your own hail risk with NOAA's Storm Prediction Center reports and FEMA's National Risk Index, and checking neighboring counties too, since hail history can look very different one county over.

After a Big Storm

If a big storm does leave a mark, DOE's advice is straightforward: if the system shows visible damage, shut it down until it gets a visual and electrical inspection, and test for electrical faults before turning it back on. Look from the ground. Don't climb on the roof to check. DOE also recommends knowing ahead of time what your insurance covers for hail, and whether there's a cap on claims.
